| [LIT-008](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-008.md) v2 | Modeling and solving an integrated periodic vehicle routing and capacitated facility location problem in the context of solid waste collection | González et al. (2025), [ARXIV-2504.10648](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.10648). The paper couples bin-capacity choice with weekly periodic capacitated routing (Sunday off, cyclic). Service time depends on the chosen bin combination, which gives an MIQP; a Glover linearisation turns it into a MILP. It solves both with Gurobi 10 for 8 h, and also with a binary-mask + permutation GA (CX 0.8, EM 0.05, pop 100, 10,000 generations). On five 12-point instances Gurobi stops at 26–32% optimality gaps. The best-of-30 GA overall cost is on average −0.08% vs the MILP incumbent and +1.70% vs the MIQP incumbent; the GA mean or median is +3.75% and +5.61%. The GA routes better (−5.75% and −5.74% routing cost) but buys much more bin capacity (+19.88% and +22.59%). On 40–163-point Bahía Blanca instances the GA returns feasible solutions in 0.72–5.58 h per run, with no bound to compare against. | Active — read in full 2026-09-25 (NOTE-015); worth reading narrowly, for its formulation (Eqs. 1–2m, with the linearisation in 3a–5) and its public Bahía Blanca instances. | [LIT-050](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-050.md) v2 | Mean-Field-Type Game Theory with Rosenblatt Noise | Tembine et al. (2025), [ARXIV-2506.08025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.08025). The paper's control and game results use linear state feedback, and they depend on the Rosenblatt noise only through its covariance, which is exactly fBM's with the same H. They are therefore identical to the fBM results. The ergodic LQ gain (Thm 4), K̂ = −[b₁ + √(b₁² + 4H(1−H)b₂²q/r)]/(2b₂(1−H)), is correct and reduces to the Brownian LQR gain at H = ½. But the paper's headline "suboptimality of noise approximation" (§VI-A, repeated for the variance-aware control, zero-sum, non-zero-sum and MFTG settings) holds only against surrogates with a different covariance; against fBM with the same H it is false. The ML claim that Rosenblatt "super-diffusion transformers" "significantly enhance the performance of generative machine intelligence models" (§XIV-C) has no model, training, dataset or experiment behind it anywhere in the paper. | Rejected — read in full 2026-09-25 (NOTE-068); not worth a reader's time. The control-theoretic results are earlier papers' (its refs [43]–[46]) restated. Its central new claim, that Gaussian and fBM surrogates give suboptimal control, is false for fBM with matching H, since the costs depend only on covariance. Its empirical sections are unsourced vignettes: numbers without references, "Rosenblatt shape" fits without any fitting procedure, and data from the first author's own startups. Its ML claim is an assertion with no model or experiment. A reader wanting Rosenblatt-noise LQ control should go to Čoupek–Duncan–Maslowski–Pasik-Duncan (CDC 2018, ref [43]) and Čoupek–Duncan–Pasik-Duncan (SPA 2022, ref [27]). |

| [LIT-352](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-352.md) v2 | A numerical algorithm for block-diagonal decomposition of matrix *-algebras with application to semidefinite programming | Murota et al. The simple components are the connected components of the graph "Q_iᵀA_pQ_{i′} ≠ O" between the eigenspaces of one random combination A(r) = Σ r_pA_p. The structure theorem it relies on, Theorem 3.1(C) "if 𝒯 is irreducible then 𝒯 = Mₙ", is false over ℝ as stated. | [LIT-868](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-868.md) | A Generalized Information-Theoretic Framework for the Emergence of Hierarchical Abstractions in Resource-Limited Systems | Larsson, Maity and Tsiotras (2022), Entropy 24(6):809. Treats a pruning of a fixed quadtree as a deterministic encoder of the grid and maximises Σβ_i I(T;Y_i) − Σγ_j I(T;Z_j) − αI(T;X) over such prunings. Every term splits over interior nodes (p(t)·JS of the children's conditionals; p(t)H of the split), so a bottom-up recursion (G-tree search) returns the optimal tree with fewest leaves in linear time. Recovers the IB and IB-with-side-information trees as special cases and proves the latter is always a pruning of the former. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-676](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-676.md)); worth reading as an exact solution of a structured information-bottleneck problem: when the encoder must be a pruning of a fixed tree (here the dyadic quadtree of a grid), every information term splits over the interior nodes, a node's share of I(T;Y) being p(t) times the Jensen–Shannon divergence of its children's p(y\|·) and its share of I(T;X) being p(t)H(Π). A bottom-up recursion, G(t) = max{ΔJ(t) + Σ G(children), 0}, then returns the optimal tree with the fewest leaves for any weighted sum of relevance, irrelevance and compression terms, in time linear in the grid. A greedy top-down search can miss all the relevant information, because a node whose children predict Y alike gains nothing however much its grandchildren differ. Adding an irrelevance penalty can only prune the plain IB tree. The hierarchy is given, not found: what "emerges" is which coarse-graining of a fixed quadtree to keep. |

| [LIT-1083](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1083.md) | An Efficient, Cost-Driven Index Selection Tool for Microsoft SQL Server | Chaudhuri and Narasayya (1997), VLDB '97. The AutoAdmin tool picks at most k indexes (single- or two-column, clustered or not) for a given workload of SQL statements, minimising the unweighted sum of the optimizer's estimated costs of those statements, with hypothetical ("what-if") indexes made visible to the optimizer by loading their statistics into the catalog. Its contribution is search efficiency: candidates are restricted to indexes in some single query's best configuration, enumeration is Greedy(m, k) (an exhaustive seed of m indexes, then greedy additions), costs of most configurations are derived from a few "atomic" ones, and two-column indexes are generated only from winning single columns. On five TPC-D workloads this cut running time to 10–24% of a baseline, with estimated-cost quality 0–7% worse, and Greedy(2, 4) matched the exhaustive optimum on four of five workloads and was within 1% on the fifth. Worth reading as the founding paper of optimizer-driven ("what-if") index selection in practice: at most k indexes chosen for a fixed workload of SQL statements to minimise the unweighted sum of the optimizer's estimated costs, made affordable by per-query candidate selection, Greedy(m, k) enumeration with an exhaustive seed, derived costs from atomic configurations, and two-column indexes grown from single-column winners (4–10 times faster than a baseline, 0–7% worse by estimated cost, on five TPC-D workloads). DBDSGN chooses, for each table, one clustered (ordering) index and a set of nonclustered indices to minimise a frequency-weighted sum of per-statement costs (access, tuple update, index maintenance) plus a weighted storage term, under an optional page limit, taking every cost from the System R optimizer's own estimates rather than an external model. | [LIT-1091](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1091.md) | Selection of views to materialize in a data warehouse | Gupta (1997), ICDT '97. Gupta states view selection on general AND-OR view graphs as minimizing frequency-weighted query cost plus update-frequency-weighted maintenance cost under a space budget. Maintenance cost enters exactly one theorem: AND view graphs (each view has one way of being computed) in which every view is queried more often than it is updated. For OR view graphs, which include Harinarayan, Rajaraman and Ullman's data cube, the paper sets update costs aside outright, so it does not add upkeep to that problem. Maintenance is an abstract per-update charge for keeping a view consistent. Worth reading as the general statement of view selection: AND-OR view graphs with query and update frequencies, and an objective of frequency-weighted query cost plus update-frequency-weighted maintenance cost under a space budget, with greedy guarantees of 1 − 1/e of the optimal benefit when space may overrun. For [QUESTION-114](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-114.md) it gives the joint objective in form: reuse against per-update upkeep under capacity. It charges no build cost, leaves the maintenance cost abstract, and models only keeping views consistent, not tolerating or acting on stale ones. Its guarantees with maintenance cost hold only for AND view graphs in which every view is queried more often than it is updated. | [LIT-1092](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1092.md) | Selection of Views to Materialize Under a Maintenance Cost Constraint | Gupta and Mumick (1999), ICDT '99. Gupta and Mumick choose views to materialize so as to minimize frequency-weighted query cost subject to a cap S on total maintenance time, the sum over chosen views of update frequency times a per-update maintenance cost that depends on which other views are stored. Because storing one view can make another cheaper to maintain, benefit per unit of maintenance is not monotone and the single-view greedy of earlier work can be arbitrarily bad. For OR view graphs (each view computed from one other, as in data cubes) a greedy that adds whole "inverted tree sets" gets at least 1 − 1/e (63%) of the benefit of an optimal solution that may use as much maintenance as the greedy did, the greedy using up to 2S, assuming no inverted-tree piece of the optimum alone exceeds S (Theorem 1, unproved here); without that assumption it gets half the optimum's benefit per unit of maintenance (Theorem 2). Each greedy stage enumerates exponentially many sets in general; for general AND-OR graphs there is only an exact A* search with exponential worst case. Upkeep is a budget, not a term traded against query savings; build cost, storage and staleness are not modelled, and the experiments are on random graphs of 10 to 25 nodes. | Active — read in full 2026-10-15 from the authors' PostScript copy on Stanford InfoLab's papers server (infolab.stanford.edu/pub/papers/update.ps, 18 pages, dated 8 October 1998, the ICDT '99 camera-ready, not the 2005 TKDE journal version; not compared with Springer's typeset pages). Worth reading as the first view-selection result that budgets maintenance time instead of space, and for its demonstration that upkeep is not additive: storing one view can make others cheaper to maintain, so benefit per unit of maintenance is not monotone and single-view greedy can be arbitrarily bad. For [QUESTION-114](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-114.md) it shows upkeep priced as a budget, U(M) = Σ update frequency × per-update maintenance cost given the other stored views, with query cost the only objective; build cost, storage and staleness are not modelled (every view is refreshed in a nightly batch). Its guarantee answers the open problem of [LIT-1091](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1091.md) only for OR view graphs: 1 − 1/e of an optimum's benefit while using up to twice the budget, under an assumption on the optimum, or half the optimum's benefit per unit of maintenance without it, with the theorems stated but not proved and a greedy whose stages are exponential in general (including on data cubes). General AND-OR graphs get only an exact A* search. It does not close the question, and comes no closer to a joint cost model than [LIT-1095](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1095.md). |
| [LIT-1094](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1094.md) | Implementing data cubes efficiently | Harinarayan, Rajaraman and Ullman (1996), SIGMOD '96. Treats a data cube's group-by queries as a lattice in which a query can be answered from any stored ancestor, prices a query at the number of rows of the smallest materialized ancestor, and chooses which views to precompute. Choosing k views to maximize the total reduction in query cost (the "benefit") is NP-complete; a greedy rule that adds the view of largest marginal benefit gets at least 1 − ((k−1)/k)^k ≥ (e−1)/e ≈ 63% of the optimal benefit, a bound that is tight, holds unchanged with query-frequency weights, and weakens to 0.63 − f under a space budget when no view takes more than a fraction f of it. The cost of building views is represented only by their size, maintenance and updates are not modelled, the data are static, and the bound is on benefit, not on query cost. On TPC-D data the greedy order reaches nearly the minimum total query time with five views and barely more space than the base view. | Active — read in full 2026-10-15 from the authors' 25-page version on Stanford InfoLab's papers server (infolab.stanford.edu/pub/papers/cube.ps, TeX run of 8 January 1996), not the SIGMOD typesetting, which the ACM Digital Library refused (403); the two were not compared. Worth reading as the standard source on choosing which precomputed answers to store when each query is answered from its cheapest stored ancestor: the lattice of group-by views, the linear cost model (rows of the ancestor scanned), NP-completeness, and a greedy rule whose total benefit, the saving against storing the base view alone, is at least 1 − ((k−1)/k)^k ≥ (e−1)/e ≈ 63% of the optimum for a budget of k views, tight, unchanged with fixed query frequencies, and only 0.63 − f under a space budget when no view exceeds a fraction f of it. The paper poses Online View Selection for a web server whose database takes updates while serving requests: choose, as the workload runs, which page fragments (WebViews) to keep stored and refreshed on every update and which to cache and invalidate, so as to minimize mean response time while the fraction of fresh fragments served (QoD) stays above a threshold θ. Worth reading as the first online view-selection algorithm that trades response time against a measured freshness: OVIS(θ) periodically moves up to a fixed number of page fragments between cached-and-invalidated and stored-and-refreshed, greedily, to keep the share of fresh fragments served above θ at the least response time, and materializes everything when it detects backlog. | [LIT-1109](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1109.md) | Adaptive Precision Setting for Cached Approximate Values | Olston et al. (2001), SIGMOD 2001. Olston, Loo and Widom set the width of each cached interval adaptively to minimize total refresh traffic. A narrow interval is escaped often (value-initiated refreshes, cost C_vr); a wide one is too imprecise for queries more often (query-initiated refreshes, cost C_qr). Under a model in which these probabilities go as 1/W² and W, the expected cost rate is least where ρ·P_vr = P_qr, ρ = 2C_vr/C_qr, and a rule that widens on value-initiated and narrows on query-initiated refreshes, with probabilities set by ρ, reached within 1% to 5% of the best fixed width in simulation. That the rule converges is argued, not proved. With exact copies required it matched an adaptive exact-caching algorithm, and where imprecision was allowed it beat it. Staleness is priced as refresh traffic only: there is no build cost, no cost of a wrong answer, and the interval is never wrong. | Active — read in full 2026-10-15 from the copy in the University of Pennsylvania's repository (ScholarlyCommons cis_papers 1351, repository.upenn.edu/server/api/core/bitstreams/92340f91-673c-435e-9b4e-b24072d4d96b/content), the camera-ready text with printed pages 355–366. Worth reading as the one model the record holds in which staleness and upkeep are traded in a single objective: a cached interval of width W is escaped (a pushed refresh, cost C_vr) more often when narrow and is too loose for queries (an exact fetch, cost C_qr) more often when wide, and under the paper's model the least expected cost is where ρ·P_vr = P_qr with ρ = 2C_vr/C_qr ([THEORY-386](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-386.md)); a rule that widens on one kind of refresh and narrows on the other came within 1–5% of the best fixed width in simulation and, restricted to exact copies, matched an adaptive cache-or-not algorithm ([THEORY-377](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-377.md)). For [QUESTION-114](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-114.md) it prices staleness as refresh traffic, with no build cost, no stored answers and no cost of a wrong answer, since the source guarantees validity. For [CLAIM-303](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-303.md) it gives upkeep and per-use verification a common dial, but only where a source sees every change; for [CLAIM-308](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-308.md) its exact-caching case is a forecast-free counting rule justified in expectation, not in the worst case, and once staleness is admitted the two-state choice becomes a continuum with an interior optimum. |
| [LIT-1117](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1117.md) | Offering a Precision-Performance Tradeoff for Aggregation Queries over Replicated Data | Olston and Widom (2000), VLDB 2000. Olston and Widom propose TRAPP: caches hold, for each numeric value, an interval its source guarantees to contain the current value, the source pushing a refresh whenever the value leaves it. A query carries a precision constraint R, and the system chooses which values to fetch exactly so that the answer interval is at most R wide whatever the true values, at least total refresh cost. For SUM (and AVG without a predicate) that choice is a 0/1 knapsack problem, NP-complete in general and polynomial with equal costs; COUNT and MIN have simple rules. Staleness becomes bounded imprecision, never error, and the cost of the source-side upkeep that guarantees this, and of setting the bound widths, is outside the optimization. The one experiment is 90 stock prices with random costs. | Active — read in full 2026-10-15 from the VLDB Endowment's open copy of the proceedings paper (www.vldb.org/conf/2000/P144.pdf, pp. 144–155; the server needs a browser User-Agent). Worth reading as the source of the idea that a cached value can be held as an interval its source guarantees, so that staleness becomes a bounded, stated imprecision instead of an unknown error, and a query buys precision down by paying for exact reads; for SUM, choosing the cheapest reads that meet a width R is a 0/1 knapsack problem ([THEORY-364](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-364.md)). For [QUESTION-114](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-114.md) it gives staleness a unit (bound width against a query's tolerance) and prices only the query side: the source's upkeep that makes the bound a guarantee, and the choice of bound widths, are assumed and uncosted, imprecision is a hard constraint rather than a loss, and a stale read can never be wrong. For [CLAIM-303](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-303.md) it sharpens "verification" into a per-use decision against a stated tolerance, but rests on a source that watches every copy, which a filed argument lacks, so it does not price the cost of reusing an obsolete conclusion; it does not bear on [CLAIM-308](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-308.md)'s rent-or-buy argument. [LIT-1109](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1109.md) prices the upkeep side. |
| [LIT-1118](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1118.md) | WebView Materialization | Labrinidis and Roussopoulos (2000), SIGMOD 2000. For a page built from database queries, the paper compares three ways to serve it on a server with online updates: compute it on each request (virt), store the query result in the DBMS and refresh it on every update (matdb), or store the finished page as a file at the web server and rewrite it on every update (matweb). It gives a cost model summing access and update costs by their frequencies and states the selection problem (choose a policy per page to minimize mean response time, no space limit, no staleness allowed), but gives no algorithm for it. On one Apache/Informix testbed with cheap indexed queries, matweb answered 10 to 230 times faster than the other two at all loads tried, and matdb was slower than virt whenever there were updates, because reading the stored result cost about as much as recomputing it. Staleness is defined as the delay from update to reply, sketched, and never measured; build cost and storage are outside the model. | Active — read in full 2026-10-15 ([NOTE-908](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-908.md)) from the authors' camera-ready copy on the University of Maryland Opsis project page (www.cs.umd.edu/projects/opsis/papers/2000/webviews.pdf, 12 pp., dated 1 March 2000); the ACM Digital Library copy returned 403. Worth reading as the first cost model for choosing, per database-generated web page, between computing it on request, storing the query result in the DBMS, and storing the finished page at the web server, with every stored copy refreshed on each update; on one Apache/Informix testbed the page stored at the web server answered 10 to 230 times faster, and the result stored in the DBMS lost to recomputation whenever there were updates, because reading it cost about as much as rebuilding it. For [QUESTION-114](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-114.md) it prices access and upkeep by frequency and adds where the copy is stored, but forbids staleness, has no build cost or storage term, and states the selection problem without an algorithm; for [CLAIM-303](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-303.md) it shows filing failing through access cost alone, and upkeep slowing the unfiled reads that share its resource (by 236% in its model check). |
| [LIT-1119](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1119.md) | Synchronizing a Database to Improve Freshness | Cho and Garcia-Molina (2000), SIGMOD 2000. For a local copy of N items, each changing as an independent Poisson process with a known rate and refreshed at fixed intervals under a fixed total refresh rate, refreshing every item equally keeps the copy fresher and younger on average than refreshing in proportion to change rate, under any distribution of rates (proved in the technical report by convexity). The freshness-optimal allocation is neither: it rises and then falls with change rate, and gives no refresh at all to items that change too fast for the budget, while the age-optimal allocation rises slowly with change rate. On estimates from 270 web sites, proportional, uniform and optimal refresh give freshness 0.12, 0.57 and 0.62. Every item matters equally, staleness is a time average with no access or query model, the refresh budget is fixed rather than priced, and refresh, change and its detection are free of any other cost. | Active — read in full 2026-10-15 from the conference version as published, the PDF of SIGMOD 2000 pp. 117–128 served by ACM SIGMOD's SIGMOD Record site for the June 2000 proceedings issue (sigmodrecord.org/publications/sigmodRecord/0006/pdfs/Synchronizing%20a%20Database%20to%20Improve%20Freshness.pdf), with the proofs it defers checked in the authors' 1999 Stanford technical report as hosted on a KTH course page. Worth reading as the standard definition of a copy's freshness and age under Poisson change, and for the result that, under a fixed refresh budget, refreshing every item equally beats refreshing in proportion to change rate for any distribution of rates, while the freshness-optimal allocation gives nothing to items that change too fast to follow. For [QUESTION-114](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-114.md) it is the first reading that prices staleness instead of forbidding it, but as an objective under a fixed budget, with no reads, no query savings and no build cost, so it supplies the staleness term and not the joint model; for [CLAIM-303](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-303.md) it models the re-checking term per unit time and by rate of change, not per use, and does not price the cost of a stale use. |
| [LIT-1155](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1155.md) v2 | The geometry of graphs and some of its algorithmic applications | Linial, London & Rabinovich (1995), *Combinatorica* 15(2): 215–245. Every n-point metric embeds in O(log n)-dimensional Euclidean space with distortion O(log n) (Bourgain's theorem as Theorem 3.2(1) states it). The paper reproves the distortion by a randomized map to distances from O(log² n) random sets, takes the dimension from Johnson–Lindenstrauss, and computes the least Euclidean distortion of any finite metric by semidefinite programming. Constant-degree expanders need distortion Ω(log n) in ℓ_p, 1 ≤ p ≤ 2, of any dimension (Proposition 4.2), so the bound is tight. The max-flow/min-cut gap for k commodities is O(log k), with a deterministic algorithm (Theorem 4.1). | Active — read 2026-10-16 ([NOTE-928](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-928.md)) in full; worth reading as the place where Bourgain's O(log n) embedding of finite metrics into Euclidean space is restated, reproved by distances to random sets of every scale, and shown tight: constant-degree expanders need distortion Ω(log n) in ℓ_p, 1 ≤ p ≤ 2, of any dimension, because their gap between multicommodity flow and cut is Ω(log n). The same embeddings bound that gap by O(log k) for k commodities. Read it knowing that the O(log n) dimension comes from Johnson–Lindenstrauss, not from the construction, which uses O(log² n) coordinates; that the lower bound rests on Leighton and Rao's gap, cited; that constants are unspecified; and that it says nothing about trees in ℓ₂, for which Sala et al. cite it. Filed as [THEORY-394](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-394.md). |
| [LIT-1212](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1212.md) v2 | Multiple-gradient descent algorithm (MGDA) for multiobjective optimization | Désidéri (2012; first as an INRIA report, 2009). A point is Pareto-stationary when some convex combination of the criteria's gradients is zero, which every Pareto-optimal point is; when a point is not, minus the minimum-norm element of the gradients' convex hull is a descent direction common to all smooth criteria, and steepest descent along it (MGDA) has a subsequence converging to a Pareto-stationary point when the criteria are positive and coercive. | Active — read 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1401](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1401.md)) in full, from the Comptes Rendus Mathématique's own open copy of the 2012 note; worth reading as the short published source for Pareto-stationarity and for the minimum-norm point of the gradients' convex hull as a common descent direction, the constructive half of [CLAIM-366](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-366.md)'s convex-hull test. Read it knowing that it does not state the converse (zero in the hull excludes common strict descent), that its convergence theorem's proof is a sketch, and that the direction, unlike its existence, depends on how the gradients are scaled, which the author leaves open. |
| [LIT-1217](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1217.md) v2 | Practical Byzantine Fault Tolerance | Castro & Liskov (1999), OSDI '99, pp. 173–186. A state-machine replication protocol that keeps safety with at most f of 3f + 1 replicas Byzantine-faulty and no timing assumption, using weak synchrony only for liveness, with MACs in place of signatures in the normal case. A Byzantine-fault-tolerant NFS on four replicas ran the Andrew benchmark 3% slower than Digital Unix's NFS, measured without faults and with view changes not yet implemented. | Active — read 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1356](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1356.md)) in full, from the copy MIT's 6.824 course hosts (pdos.csail.mit.edu), the proceedings text of pp. 173–186; worth reading as the paper that made Byzantine-fault-tolerant state-machine replication practical: safety with at most f of 3f + 1 replicas faulty and no timing assumption, liveness under weak synchrony, a faulty primary replaced by rotation rather than by voting anyone out. Read it knowing that correct behaviour is defined as following the protocol, so the service's own specification is taken as given; that its fault bound needs independent failures the paper says must be engineered; and that its measurements are of the normal case on four replicas, with view changes not implemented in the measured library. |

For uncertain LPs with here-and-now and wait-and-see variables, the Adjustable Robust Counterpart (∀ data ∃ adjustment) is never more conservative than the usual Robust Counterpart (∃ one solution ∀ data), coincides with it under constraint-wise uncertainty, and is usually NP-hard. Restricting adjustments to affine functions of the data gives a tractable counterpart for fixed recourse and tight semidefinite approximations otherwise. Each decision may have an information basis, the part of the data it may depend on; in an inventory model, poorer bases raise cost and the non-adjustable counterpart is infeasible. | Active — read 2026-11-03 ([NOTE-1503](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1503.md)), from the published text on A. | [LIT-2023](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2023.md) | A Proof of the CSP Dichotomy Conjecture | Zhuk (2017; J. ACM 2020). For a finite set of relations Γ on a finite domain, "CSP(Γ) can be solved in polynomial time if there exists a WNU preserving Γ; CSP(Γ) is NP-complete otherwise." The hardness half was known; the paper gives the algorithm. It rests on a structural theorem derived from Rosenberg's classification of maximal clones: every finite algebra with a special WNU has a nontrivial binary absorbing subuniverse, a nontrivial centre, or a proper congruence modulo which it is polynomially complete or is Z_p. The algorithm enforces cycle-consistency and irreducibility, reduces domains while keeping solvability, and in the linear case solves linear equations over prime fields, finding missing equations by recursive calls. Proved independently of Bulatov ([LIT-2115](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2115.md)), by a different algorithm. | Active — read in part 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1555](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1555.md)) from arXiv v11, which the author marks as the final version; worth reading as the second independent proof of the CSP dichotomy, stated in exactly the terms the pasted synthesis uses (a WNU "preserving Γ"), with an algorithm that needs only local consistency and linear equations over prime fields, and for its §10, the clearest list of what the theorem leaves open: infinite domains, where CSPs can be undecidable, quantified CSPs, whose classification fails to be a clean dichotomy, and a truly polynomial algorithm. Its main limits: finite domain and finite language only, decision only, nothing on moving between solutions, exponential in the domain size, and a proof of some 55 pages (§§6–9) not checked here. |

Gopalan et al.'s classification of the connectivity of Boolean solution spaces did not consider constraints in which a variable occurs more than once. Such repetitions can turn a relation with good component structure into one without it, so the dichotomies for st-connectivity, connectivity and diameter hold with "safely tight" sets, whose relations keep the property under identification of variables, in place of tight ones; the boundary moves slightly toward the hard side. | [LIT-2028](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2028.md) | Do Expiring Budgets Lead to Wasteful Year-End Spending? Evidence from Federal Procurement | Liebman & Mahoney (NBER 2013; AER 2017). A two-subperiod model of an agency with a fixed annual budget, uncertain value-of-spending shocks and concave returns: a precautionary motive makes it hold back early and exhaust the budget at year-end, including on spending worth less than the social cost of funds. In 14.6 million federal contracts, 2004–2009, 8.7 percent of spending falls in the last week of the year against about 1.9 percent in a uniform week, and I.T. projects begun in that week have 2.2 to 5.6 times higher odds of a lower quality rating. Rollover helps only if Congress commits not to claw it back; DOJ's I.T. rollover authority cut the year-end spike by 9.5 percentage points; and in a calibration a one-month grace period gives 41 percent, and a four-month one 90 percent, of the welfare gain from full rollover. | Active — read 2026-11-04 ([NOTE-1553](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1553.md)) from the authors' NBER working paper w19481, revised January 2018, main text in full, appendices skipped; worth reading as the first economic analysis of wasteful year-end spending: a model in which an expiring budget turns a precautionary buffer held against uncertain needs into low-value spending at the deadline, evidence of the spending spike and of lower-quality year-end I.T. projects in US federal procurement, and a commitment analysis and calibration of rollover and grace periods. Its main limits: quality is measured only on I.T. projects that survive into the I.T. Dashboard, the DOJ quality result rests on a single last-week project, the welfare numbers depend on a CRRA calibration, and the model has no principal–agent misuse, borrowing or supplemental appropriations. |
| [LIT-2029](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2029.md) | Synthesis of Bistable Compliant Structures from Truss Mechanisms | Kinoshita & Ohsaki (2009). Bistable compliant mechanisms are easier to find as pin-jointed trusses, since optimizing frames with geometric nonlinearity failed to converge because of local buckling, but a pin- jointed truss cannot be made in one piece. A two-bar study and one seven-node example show it. | Active — read in full 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1597](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1597.md)) from the publisher's open-access PDF on J-STAGE; worth reading as a short worked case of a design found in one constraint model (pin-jointed bars, no bending) having to be re-realized in another (rigid joints with bending) by a second optimization: a bistable truss mechanism, whose second stable state is snap-through stopped by an obstacle, is converted into a single-piece frame by sizing thin end regions at the former pin joints under a strain cap, so that no point hinge forms. Its main limits: one numerical example, no fabrication or experiment, equivalence shown only by overlaid force–displacement curves, and the second stable state still rests on a placed obstacle. |

| [LIT-2052](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2052.md) | Optimization of conditional value-at-risk | Rockafellar & Uryasev (2000). For a loss f(x, y) of a decision x under random y, the function F_β(x, α) = α + (1−β)⁻¹ E[f(x, y) − α]⁺ is convex and continuously differentiable in α; its minimum over α is the β-CVaR, and the left end of its set of minimizers is the β-VaR (Theorem 1). So minimizing CVaR over x is minimizing F_β jointly over (x, α), which also yields the VaR of the optimal decision (Theorem 2): a convex program when the loss is convex in x, and a linear program on sampled scenarios when it is linear, with no normality assumed. Illustrated on a three-asset portfolio under normal returns, where minimum-CVaR, minimum-VaR and minimum-variance portfolios coincide, and on hedging a NIKKEI options portfolio with a non-normal loss. | Active — read in full 2026-11-04 ([NOTE-1623](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1623.md)) from the authors' manuscript of 1999-09-05, posted on Rockafellar's own publications page at the University of Washington, not the typeset journal version; worth reading as the paper that turns conditional value-at-risk from a quantity defined through value-at-risk into the minimum of a convex function of one extra scalar, so that minimizing it over decisions is a convex program, and on sampled scenarios with linear losses a linear program, with the VaR obtained as a byproduct. Its limits: it assumes a loss distribution with no atoms, works in one period at a fixed confidence level with a known or simulable distribution, and its evidence of numerical quality is two small examples, in one of which pseudo-random sampling at β = 0.99 is off by up to about 5% in CVaR. |
| [LIT-2053](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2053.md) v2 | Urban Operations Research | Larson & Odoni (1981), a textbook; only chapter 5 was read, §5.4 in full. The hypercube model represents an urban service with N distinguishable units over a city split into atoms, each an independent Poisson source of calls. Each unit is busy or free, so the state is a vertex of an N-cube; dispatch follows a fixed preference list per atom. From the steady state the authors compute each unit's workload, the fraction of dispatches sending each unit to each atom, the dispatches across response areas and the mean travel times. Workload sharing makes the units' workloads more even than those of their response areas. Exact solution needs 2^N equations; Larson's approximation needs N. | Active — read 2026-11-06 (NOTE-1620, Read): chapter 5 §5.4 in full with its equations, tables and figures, the opening of §5.5 and §5.3.5, from the online edition the authors post at MIT as a course supplement; the rest of the book was not read. Worth reading as the authors' own textbook statement of the hypercube queueing model of urban emergency services: N distinguishable units, each busy or free, on the vertices of an N-cube; geographical atoms as Poisson sources; fixed-preference dispatch; the nine assumptions; and the unit workloads, inter-district dispatch fractions and travel times computed from the steady state, with Larson's N-equation approximation. Registered as the stand-in for Larson (1974), [LIT-2105](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2105.md), whose model it restates and cites. Its main limits: the basic model evaluates the response areas a user supplies rather than optimizing them; priority dispatching is excluded; one unit is sent per call; exact computation grows as 2^N. |
| [LIT-2054](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2054.md) | Quantitative Foundations for Resource Theories | Marsden & Zwart (CSL 2018). "We present a categorical foundation for quantitative resource theories, derived from enriched category theory." Conversions are enriched in a commutative quantale Q: "The monoid structure allows us to combine quantities across the different steps of a process or algorithm", and "The join semilattice structure is then an optimizer." The Lawvere quantale ([0, ∞], inf, +) gives costs, the interval quantale with min connection strengths, the multiplicative one success probabilities. Free conversions are the base Q-categories, costly ones Q-profunctors; five free constructions (monoidal, symmetric, deleting, copying, cartesian) give comonads for many-to-one conversions, and every endomorphism generates a free internal monad by reflexive–transitive closure. | Active — read in full 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1602](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1602.md)) from the publisher's open-access PDF on Dagstuhl's LIPIcs site; worth reading as the categorical foundation for quantitative resource theories: conversions enriched in a commutative quantale, whose monoid combines the costs, probabilities or connection strengths of successive steps and whose join picks the best alternative, with costly conversions as profunctors and closure under composition as a free internal monad (reflexive–transitive closure). Its main limits: one quantale per theory, so a product of quantities keeps only componentwise optima; static resources; proofs sketched. Probably, not certainly, the Oxford University Research Archive item the pasted synthesis cites; ORA itself could not be searched (Cloudflare). |
| [LIT-2056](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2056.md) v2 | Planning and acting in partially observable stochastic domains | Kaelbling, Littman & Cassandra (1998). An agent that cannot observe the state keeps a belief state, a probability distribution over states updated by Bayes' rule, which is a sufficient statistic for its history; control then becomes an MDP over beliefs. The optimal t-step value is the upper surface of one linear function per policy tree, so it is piecewise-linear and convex, and the optimal policy partitions belief space into polyhedral regions. The paper adds the witness algorithm and the tiger problem, where with two steps to go the optimal policy only listens. It credits Smallwood and Sondik with the belief state's sufficiency (jointly with another work) and an exact direct-construction algorithm that is exponential in the worst case. | Active — read 2026-11-04 and 2026-11-06 (NOTE-1563, Read for the parts on the belief state and the value function) from the published PDF on the first author's MIT CSAIL page; worth reading as the standard restatement, for an AI readership, of the operations-research theory of partially observable Markov decision processes: the belief state as a sufficient statistic, control as an MDP over beliefs, the piecewise-linear convex finite-horizon value function, and the tiger problem, in which a costly, noisy information action is valued inside the model. Registered as the stand-in for Smallwood and Sondik (1973), [LIT-2038](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2038.md), whose core finite-horizon results it restates. Its main limits: enumerated rather than factored states, a known model, and exact solution intractable in general. |
| [LIT-2059](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2059.md) v2 | Economies-of-Scale in Many-Server Queueing Systems: Tutorial and Partial Review of the QED Halfin–Whitt Heavy-Traffic Regime | van Leeuwaarden, Mathijsen & Zwart (2019). A tutorial on many-server systems in the Quality-and-Efficiency-Driven regime. With s = λ + β√λ servers, the extra capacity is of the order of the load's natural fluctuations; under that scaling, and only under it, the M/M/s delay probability tends to a limit strictly between zero and one, and the scaled number in system tends to the Halfin–Whitt diffusion. Load per server tends to one while the mean delay vanishes at rate 1/√s: large pooled systems need proportionally less spare capacity. The limits give staffing rules for delay targets and costs that, in the authors' figures, differ from the exact optimum by at most one server. | Active — read 2026-11-04 and 2026-11-06 (NOTE-1577, Read for the parts on the M/M/s results) from arXiv v2; worth reading as a clear tutorial on the Quality-and-Efficiency-Driven (Halfin–Whitt) regime: the square-root staffing rule s = λ + β√λ, Halfin and Whitt's theorem that the M/M/s delay probability has a non-degenerate limit exactly under that scaling, the diffusion limit, the economies of scale that let utilization approach one while service stays good, and dimensioning rules for service targets and costs. Registered as the stand-in for Halfin and Whitt (1981), [LIT-2085](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2085.md), whose M/M/s results it states and attributes. | [LIT-2063](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2063.md) | Computational Complexities of Folding | Eppstein (2025). Flat-folding a finite crease pattern is fixed-parameter tractable in ply and the treewidth of a cell adjacency graph, and under the exponential time hypothesis the singly-exponential dependence on treewidth cannot be improved, even for bounded ply. The 3D shape folded from a triangulated net with integer edge lengths cannot always be computed by radicals or bounded-degree roots (a Galois-theoretic result). In a toy model of squares hinged at one edge to a tabletop, moving from one flat state to another one square at a time is PSPACE-complete, by reduction from nondeterministic constraint logic, and counting flat states is #P-complete. For self-similar crease patterns with infinitely many creases on a finite square, flat-foldability is undecidable. | Active — read 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1611](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1611.md)) from the publisher's open PDF on J-STAGE, main text and every theorem statement in full, the binary-tiling gadgets of §6.3–6.6 and the proofs of Lemmas 7–10 skimmed; worth reading as a map of how the complexity of folding depends on the question asked: deciding flat-foldability of a finite crease pattern is fixed-parameter tractable in ply and treewidth, with an ETH-optimal dependence on treewidth; exact 3D folded shapes can need numbers no radical or bounded-degree root computation reaches; reaching one flat state from another in the "flaps and flips" toy model is PSPACE-complete and counting its states #P-complete; and flat-foldability of self-similar patterns with infinitely many creases is undecidable. The NP-completeness of flat folding it cites is earlier work, not its own. Its main limits: flaps and flips are uncreased squares taped to a table, a toy and not one folded sheet; the moves are discrete, with no mechanics; and the undecidability needs infinitely many creases. |
| [LIT-2066](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2066.md) v2 | Policies for the Operation of an Ambulance Fleet under Uncertainty based on a New Preparedness Metric | Guigues, Kleywegt & Nascimento (2026). An EMS repeatedly chooses which ambulance to send to a new call, or to queue it, and where a newly free ambulance goes, to a queued call or a station; each choice affects readiness for calls not yet known. The paper defines a station-level preparedness metric, the steady-state cost rate of a continuous-time Markov chain over the station's busy ambulances by ambulance and emergency type, computed offline for every supply vector, and makes each decision by a small integer program trading immediate response cost, queueing penalty and a weighted change in preparedness. In a Rio de Janeiro simulation this policy had lower mean allocation cost than nine published policies in most cases, and on mean response time was usually behind four of them. | Active — read in full 2026-11-06 (NOTE-1567, Read) from the arXiv preprint, v1; worth reading as a clear statement of the two recurring EMS decisions, which ambulance to send or whether to queue a call, and where a freed ambulance goes, with the trade-off that serving a call now lowers readiness for calls not yet known, and for its station-level preparedness metric, the steady-state cost rate of a Markov chain over a station's busy ambulances, used inside a one-step integer program. In a Rio de Janeiro simulation the resulting policy had the lowest mean allocation cost against nine published policies in most configurations, but seldom the lowest mean response time. Its main limits: an unrefereed preprint; a local, per-station approximation the authors say may fail when demand is large relative to supply; assumed allocation costs, which the authors call examples, not guidelines; one city; and no comparison with the approximate dynamic programming policies. | [LIT-2071](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2071.md) | Rigid Foldability is NP-Hard | Akitaya, Demaine, Horiyama, Hull, Ku & Tachi (2020). Deciding whether a crease pattern folds rigidly from flat is weakly NP-hard using all creases, by a reduction from Partition, and strongly NP-hard with optional creases, by one from 1-in-3 SAT. The model takes belcastro and Hull's condition, that crease rotations multiply to the identity around every closed vertex-avoiding curve, as necessary and, near flat, sufficient. Flat-foldable degree-4 vertices fold in two modes linear in tan(ρ/2), so foldability reduces to choosing modes so that around every face the fold-speed coefficients multiply to 1 (Corollary 11); the hardness is in that combinatorial choice, not in self-intersection. | Active — read 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1579](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1579.md)) from the arXiv preprint, model and main text in full and the reduction gadgets skimmed; worth reading as the proof that deciding whether a crease pattern folds rigidly from flat is weakly NP-hard when every crease must fold and strongly NP-hard when creases are optional, and for its clear statement of belcastro and Hull's loop condition (the crease rotations met along any closed vertex-avoiding curve multiply to the identity): necessary, not sufficient because the paper may cross itself, and sufficient near the flat state. The hardness lies in choosing a folding mode at each vertex so that every face closes. Registered as a stand-in for the unread belcastro and Hull (2002), [LIT-2067](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2067.md), and for the NP-hardness section of the unread chapter "Rigid Origami Theory" of Hull's Origametry, [LIT-2087](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2087.md). Its main limits: the bound is not shown tight, membership in NP is open in general, and foldability ignores mechanics. |
| [LIT-2073](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2073.md) v2 | Connectivity of spaces of directed paths in geometric models for concurrent computation | Raussen (2021; Computational Geometry 2023). In Dijkstra's PV model, n processors lock and release shared resources, "Any resource r ∈ R has capacity to serve up to κ(r) ∈ N of these processors at any given time", and the state space is the product of the processors' time intervals minus the forbidden region where some resource is over capacity. Executions are directed paths in it, and d-homotopic executions give the same result. A spare capacity κ(X), computed from the program text and the capacities, bounds the connectivity of every space of executions to the target: (κ(X) − 2)-connected (Theorem 4.3). So κ = 0 exactly at deadlocks, κ(X) ≥ 1 excludes them, and κ(X) ≥ 2 makes all executions equivalent. | Active — read in full 2026-11-05 and 2026-11-06 (NOTE-1581) from arXiv v3, as the neighbour standing in for Fajstrup, Goubault & Raussen 2006 ([LIT-2065](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2065.md)), which could not be fetched. Worth reading as a clear, recent statement of the geometric model of concurrency, in which shared resources of fixed capacity cut a forbidden region out of the product of the processors' time intervals, executions are directed paths around it, and equivalent executions are d-homotopic; and for its result that a spare capacity computed from the program text bounds the connectivity of every space of executions, so that zero marks deadlocks and two or more makes all executions equivalent. Its main limits: linear PV programs only (loops by unfolding), lower bounds attained at a vertex of minimal spare capacity and otherwise not tight, algorithms sketched; a research paper on one question, not a survey of directed homotopy. |

| [LIT-2076](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2076.md) | Distinguishing Useful and Wasteful Slack | Bogetoft & Kerstens (online 2022; Operations Research 72(4), 2024). Unverified until read: from the abstract only. Organization and strategic-management studies hold that slack may be useful, as a buffer against environmental shocks, to decouple organizations, to ease planning and implementation, to support innovation and to respond to competitors; economics tends to see it as wasteful. The paper aims to separate the two by a Pareto criterion: if an organization could keep the same outputs and the same slack at lower cost, the excess spending is wasteful, or nonrationalizable. It measures how much of total spending can be rationalized and tests the usefulness of the available slack statistically by bootstrapping. Unread. | Unfetched — searched 2026-11-04 for a lawful full text; copies exist but this client could not fetch them, so it is not read and no NOTE is filed. The article is CC BY.
