Unpaywall not used, since it requires an email address. The tutorial of van Leeuwaarden, Mathijsen and Zwart (2019), [LIT-2059](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2059.md), stands in for it on the M/M/s results (the square-root scaling, the condition for a non-degenerate delay probability and its limit, the diffusion limit and its stationary distribution), stated and attributed but not proved; it does not stand in for the original's proofs, its other models, its numerical work or its own framing. The record's account of this paper's M/M/s results is a report of the tutorial, THEORY-1416, which attributes to Halfin and Whitt the condition (1 − ρ)√s → β for a non-degenerate delay probability, its limit g(β), the diffusion limit that is a negative-drift Brownian motion above full occupancy and an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process below it, and its stationary distribution. Until this paper is read, those are attributions, not readings. A web search on 2026-11-06 found no lawful copy. |
| [LIT-2089](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2089.md) | Ambulance location for maximum survival | Erkut, Ingolfsson & Erdoğan (2008). Takes the real objective of an EMS to be survivors, with coverage within a time standard a proxy, and replaces 0–1 coverage in four standard location models (MCLP, MEXCLP and their probabilistic-response versions) with a survival function for out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. On Edmonton data (180 demand points, 16 candidate sites), evaluated with the approximate hypercube model, maximal-covering locations give up to 7.7% fewer expected survivors and q-median locations up to 23.5% fewer than survival-maximizing ones in the deterministic models; with random response times the gain averages 0.9%, and in the model with both random response times and busy probabilities it adds little. Locating to minimize average response time does worse still, by 6.5% on average against the full survival model. | Active — read in full 2026-11-04 ([NOTE-1556](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1556.md)) from the accepted preprint of November 2007 posted on the second author's University of Alberta page; worth reading as the argument, with a pathological example, that 0–1 coverage within a time standard is a poor proxy for the real objective of an EMS, survivors, and as the construction of survival-maximizing versions of four standard covering models, compared on Edmonton data. The switch to a survival objective gives up to 7.7% more expected survivors than maximal covering and up to 23.5% more than the q-median in the deterministic models, and the gap shrinks once random response times or busy probabilities enter the coverage model. Its main limits: survival functions for cardiac arrest only, assumed to hold for all urgent calls; static location models with no dispatch or relocation; one city. Filed as a stand-in for McLay and Mayorga (2010), [LIT-2090](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2090.md), for the shared idea only; it partly pulls against that paper's headline. |
| [LIT-2090](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2090.md) | Evaluating emergency medical service performance measures | McLay & Mayorga (2010). Unverified until read: from the abstract only. Most EMS systems are measured by the share of calls reached within a response-time threshold, not by patient outcomes, because thresholds "are easy to obtain and to understand". The paper evaluates thresholds by the patient survival their optimal ambulance locations yield, against a model that locates ambulances to maximize survival, on data from Hanover County, Virginia. The abstract reports that locating for seven- and eight-minute thresholds also maximizes survival, while nine- and ten-minute thresholds give more equitable outcomes, with better rural survival. A cites it for the operational metric not being the organizational objective; the abstract's headline is a convergence at one threshold, with the divergence about equity. | Unavailable — registered 2026-11-04 from the pasted bibliography on emergency readiness, and no lawful full text was found. Crossref and PubMed (PMID 20629415, abstract only; no PMC copy) were read for the bibliography and abstract. OpenAlex (W1994976571) gives OA status closed and lists Springer (paywalled), PubMed, a handle resolving to the DOI and a CiteSeerX record (10.1.1.541.3392), whose API redirected to the Internet Archive and was reset; CiteSeerX names no author or institutional host, so it would not have counted as an author copy. Searches of the authors' pages and of .edu hosts found no copy; Academia.edu and ResearchGate (login walls) were not used. Stands in for it, for the idea and not the results: Erkut, Ingolfsson and Erdoğan (2008), [LIT-2089](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2089.md), read in [NOTE-1556](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1556.md), which argues more strongly that coverage within a time standard is a proxy for survivors and compares survival-maximizing with covering locations on Edmonton data; it partly pulls against this paper's headline, finding that a realistic enough coverage model reaches the survival optimum but that plain coverage "should not be used for EMS vehicle location". It has none of this paper's Hanover County findings. No NOTE is filed. |
| [LIT-2092](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2092.md) v2 | A multi-period and bi-objective approach for locating ambulances: a case study in Belo Horizonte, Brazil | de Oliveira, de Sá & Martins (2020). Multi-period forms of two ambulance-location models, the deterministic FLEET and Sorensen and Church's local-reliability expected covering model, let ambulances move among bases between periods in Belo Horizonte's emergency medical service, and a bi-objective form trades the number of bases against coverage. The abstract reports coverage up to 31 and 24 points higher than the 2019 configuration; relocation with the bases held fixed adds at most 1.7 points. Its §2 restates MEXCLP and MALP: expected coverage under uniform busyness and independence, and coverage with reliability α from area-specific busy fractions. | Active — read in full 2026-11-06 ([NOTE-1621](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1621.md), Read) from arXiv v1. Worth reading for multi-period forms of FLEET and of the local-reliability expected covering model LR-MEXCLP, in which ambulances change bases between periods, with a bases-against-coverage bi-objective form, applied to Belo Horizonte's emergency medical service, and for §2's compact account of MEXCLP, MALP and LR-MEXCLP. Registered as a stand-in for Daskin (1983), [LIT-2098](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2098.md), and ReVelle and Hogan (1989), [LIT-2075](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2075.md), on what those models maximize and assume. Its main limits: a preprint; one city; costless relocation; reported relocation gains that mostly come from optimizing the bases; probabilistic coverage rates that cannot be reproduced from the stated objective. |
| [LIT-2095](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2095.md) | Real-Time Ambulance Dispatching and Relocation | Nasrollahzadeh, Khademi & Mayorga (2018). Unverified until read: from the abstract only. Real-time ambulance dispatching and relocation, in which the decision maker may "(i) select any available ambulance to dispatch to a call or to queue the call and (ii) send an idle ambulance to cover the location of an ambulance just dispatched to a call", formulated as a stochastic dynamic program and solved approximately (ADP) because the state space is unbounded. Lower bounds on expected response time and on the expected fraction of late calls of any relocation policy are used to judge the policies. In a Mecklenburg County, North Carolina case study the abstract reports that the ADP policy cuts expected response time by 12% and the fraction of late high-priority calls by 30.6% against the best static benchmarks. A cites it for the value of availability; the abstract says nothing of provisional dispatch or cancellation en route. | Unavailable — registered 2026-11-04 from the pasted bibliography on emergency readiness, and no lawful full text was found. Crossref and OpenAlex (W2797681513) list only the publisher's paywalled landing page, with OA status closed and no repository copy. The first author's Clemson PhD dissertation, Approximate Dynamic Programming: Health Care Applications (2019), whose abstract describes "The dynamic programming formulation for real-time ambulance dispatching and relocation policies" and so probably carries this paper as a chapter (unverified), has a record page at https://open.clemson.edu/all_dissertations/2343/; its PDF, https://open.clemson.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=3347&context=all_dissertations, returned 403 with a Cloudflare challenge and was not retried. ResearchGate (login wall) and a commercial translation-sales site were not used. Stands in for it, weakly: Guigues, Kleywegt and Nascimento (2026), [LIT-2066](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2066.md), which states the same problem class (choose any available ambulance or queue the call; reassign a freed ambulance) and describes this paper in two sentences, but gives none of its formulation, bounds or results and does not compare against its policy. No NOTE is filed. |
| [LIT-2096](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2096.md) v2 | Rational Inefficiencies | Bogetoft & Hougaard (working paper 2001, revised 2002; J. Productivity Analysis 2003). Measured technical inefficiency, excess inputs or slack, is treated not as waste but as a rational choice: the organization values off-the-job profit and on-the-job slack and chooses slack under its control regime. Under a price-based regime it uses an allocatively efficient underlying plan and takes the rest of the budget as profit and slack; under a restriction-based regime the underlying plan is technically efficient and supported by endogenous prices. Observed inputs then constrain, by revealed preference, how it trades profit against slack and one kind of slack against another. Since the gains from slack are unknown, inefficiency cannot be concluded to be waste to be eliminated; which slack is valuable is posed as an open problem. | Active — read in full 2026-11-06 (NOTE-1576, Read) from the 2001 working paper, revised July 2002, deposited in AgEcon Search; worth reading as the case that measured technical inefficiency can be a rational choice of on-the-job slack, with the organizational motives for slack, and as a revealed-preference way of reading an organization's slack trade-offs from its input use. Registered as a stand-in for Bogetoft and Kerstens (2022), [LIT-2076](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2076.md), whose premise it states and whose results it does not. Its main limits: a single aggregate value function whose owner is left open, convexity needed for key results, only partial identification without parametric aggregators, no empirical application, and the useful–wasteful distinction posed, not solved. |
| [LIT-2098](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2098.md) | A Maximum Expected Covering Location Model: Formulation, Properties and Heuristic Solution | Daskin (1983). Unverified until read; from the abstract on Crossref. The maximal covering location model is extended to allow that a demand may go uncovered because every facility able to cover it is busy serving other demands: "The model is extended to account for the chance that when a demand arrives at the system it will not be covered since all facilities capable of covering the demand are engaged serving other demands." An integer program is given, "Several properties of the formulation are proven", and a heuristic is presented with computational results. The neighbours add that the objective is expected coverage, with one system-wide busy probability and independent servers. | Unavailable — not read; no lawful copy located as of 2026-11-04. Looked at: the publisher (INFORMS), paywalled, not tried beyond its listing; OpenAlex W2133676848 (oa_status closed, no repository full text); the author's University of Michigan pages, https://umich.edu/~msdaskin/ and its courses page, which returned HTTP 403 with a Cloudflare challenge and were not retried (a syllabus PDF from that site that did come back lists the paper and has no content); a linear MEXCLP formulation at https://core.ac.uk/download/301648743.pdf and a thesis restating MEXCLP at research.vu.nl, both Cloudflare challenges, not retried; arXiv searches for "maximum expected covering" and MEXCLP, which found nothing. Two neighbours stand in for it, on what the model maximizes and assumes only. De Oliveira, de Sá and Martins (2020), [LIT-2092](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2092.md), §2, state that MEXCLP maximizes expected coverage given that servers may be busy, under uniform busyness and server independence, and that it may place several ambulances to cover one demand point. Mukhopadhyay et al. (2020), [LIT-2107](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2107.md), §6.1, state that it extends the maximal covering model for station availability with one busy probability for every facility, and name its later extensions. Neither gives its objective formula, the properties it proves, its heuristic or its computational results. |
| [LIT-2099](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2099.md) | Hinge-Free Compliant Mechanism Design via the Topological Level-Set | Krishnakumar & Suresh (2015). Compliant-mechanism topology optimization must trade flexibility at the output against stiffness against a workpiece, and density-based (SIMP) designs tend to form point hinges. The authors maximize mutual strain energy over a weighted sum of input and output strain energies, the weight η trading geometric against mechanical advantage, and remove material where the topological derivative of that ratio is lowest, with fixed-point iterations at each volume fraction. Elements are in or out, so no pseudo-densities and no point hinges; one run gives designs of decreasing volume. Examples: 2D inverters, a cruncher, a grasper, a 3D inverter and flap. | Active — read in full 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1582](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1582.md)) from a manuscript posted on the second author's lab page at UW-Madison, most likely the authors' manuscript of the journal article; registered as a stand-in for Sigmund (1997), [LIT-2043](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2043.md), and more thinly for the review by Zhu et al. (2020), [LIT-2051](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2051.md). Worth reading as a compact statement of what compliant-mechanism topology optimization trades: flexibility at the output against stiffness against a workpiece, a multi-objective problem with Pareto solutions, and density-based designs that exploit the model with point hinges. Its own method removes material by the topological derivative of a mutual-to-weighted-input-and-output strain-energy ratio, avoiding pseudo-densities and hinges, with one parameter trading geometric against mechanical advantage. Its main limits: linear elasticity, coarse meshes, no springs or stress constraints, no fabrication, comparisons qualitative. |
| [LIT-2101](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2101.md) v2 | Design for Process Flexibility: Efficiency of the Long Chain and Sparse Structure | Chou, Chua, Teo & Zheng (2010). Plants and products form a bipartite graph and sales, once demand is realised, are a max-flow. For balanced, identical systems with independent demand symmetric about its mean, a generalised random walk gives the long chain's efficiency as the system grows: about 89.6% of full flexibility's expected sales for uniform demand and 96% for normal (CV 0.33), but only 58% and about 70% of its gain over dedicated plants; two-point demand gives 75% of sales. For general systems, a sparse structure sampled with suitable probabilities comes within ε of full flexibility; with correlated demand a sparse structure can serve almost none of it. The paper gives analytical support to the chaining principle that Jordan and Graves found by simulation, and reuses their 16-plant data. | Active — read 2026-11-06 (NOTE-1604, Read) from the INFORMS author-courtesy PDF on NUS Business School's site; worth reading as the analytical backing for the chaining principle of process flexibility: for balanced, identical plants and products with independent demand, the long chain keeps about 89.6% (uniform demand) and 96% (normal demand, CV 0.33) of full flexibility's expected sales as the system grows, but only 58% and about 70% of its gain over dedicated plants; in general a suitably sampled sparse structure comes within ε of full flexibility, while with correlated demand a sparse structure can lose almost everything. Registered as the stand-in for Jordan and Graves (1995), [LIT-2045](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2045.md), whose simulation findings it reports. Its main limits: a single period, lost sales, and the chain results only for balanced, independent, symmetric demand. |
| [LIT-2103](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2103.md) | Ending Wasteful Year-End Spending: On Optimal Budget Rules in Organizations | Siemroth (SSRN 2021; Essex discussion paper 2022; IER 2024). A two-year model in which an agent privately observes each year's spending need and values spending above it at α < 1, which the principal does not value at all. The principal commits in advance to a roll-over share Δ of unused funds, to audit rules and to a punishment. Without them the agent spends everything. Some roll-over is weakly better than none, and works only if Δ > α; partial roll-over can be optimal when α and the budget are small and the cost of funds large, but for most parameters full roll-over is optimal. Audits are threshold rules (audit only large spending), except an interval rule in year 1 when roll-over already induces saving; punishment is maximal and never imposed in equilibrium; and with an endogenous budget, strategic underfunding can be optimal. | Active — read 2026-11-04 ([NOTE-1594](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1594.md)) from the author's February 2022 Essex Economics Discussion Paper in the University of Essex repository, main text in full, appendix proofs skipped; the open-access version of record at Wiley returned a Cloudflare challenge, so the published text, which may differ after revision, was not read. Worth reading as the first analysis of the optimal roll-over rule for unused funds together with optimal audit rules: some roll-over is weakly better than none, it works only when the share exceeds the agent's marginal gain from misuse, partial roll-over is sometimes optimal, audits are threshold rules (an interval rule in year 1), and punishment is maximal and never imposed. Its main limits: two periods, risk-neutral parties, uniform needs for the closed forms, deterministic audits, no ratchet effect, the partial roll-over and underfunding cases shown only in restricted regions or on a small numerical grid, and no empirical test. |
| [LIT-2104](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2104.md) | On the complexity of reconfiguration problems | Ito, Demaine, Harvey, Papadimitriou, Sideri, Uehara & Uno (2011). A reconfiguration problem fixes a search problem and a symmetric adjacency on its feasible solutions, and asks whether two feasible solutions are joined by a path of feasible solutions. Reconfiguration versions of power supply, independent set, clique, vertex cover, set cover and 0–1 integer programming are PSPACE-complete; reconfiguration of matroid bases and of matchings is in P. Choosing a path to optimise its worst intermediate objective is NP-hard to approximate within any constant for maxmin clique, strongly NP-hard for minmax power supply, and has a linear-time 2-approximation for minmax set cover. | Active — read 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1595](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1595.md)) from the publisher's PDF posted on co-author Erik Demaine's own page, after ScienceDirect showed a captcha; main text in full, the matching algorithm and the proofs of Lemmas 3–4 and Theorem 7 skimmed; worth reading as the paper that defines reconfiguration problems in general and gives the first systematic map: reconfiguration versions of many NP-complete problems (power supply, independent set, clique, vertex cover, set cover, 0–1 integer programming) are PSPACE-complete, some versions of problems in P (matroid bases, matchings) are in P, and optimising the worst intermediate state (maxmin, minmax) is hard to approximate in some cases and 2-approximable in others. Probably, not certainly, the work the pasted synthesis on resource-bounded realizability cites unnamed. Its main limits: most PSPACE results are proof sketches, the questions are decision questions about whether a path exists, and adjacency is combinatorial, with no physical setting. |
| [LIT-2105](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2105.md) | A hypercube queuing model for facility location and redistricting in urban emergency services | Larson (1974). Unverified until read: no copy and no abstract were reached. As the neighbours report it, the paper introduced the hypercube queueing model of an urban emergency service, in which each of N distinguishable units is busy or free, so that the system's state is a vertex of an N-dimensional cube, and solved it exactly by an iteration over hyperplanes of states with equal numbers of busy units, with the TOUR algorithm generating the transition rates. Whether it optimizes locations or districts, as its title suggests, or evaluates configurations a user supplies, the neighbours do not say. The pasted bibliography on emergency readiness reads it as valuing a unit by the availability and states of the others; the valuation is A's. | Unavailable — not read; no lawful copy located as of 2026-11-04. Looked at: the publisher (Elsevier), paywalled, its Crossref links only TDM API endpoints, not tried; OpenAlex W2093228967 (oa_status closed, no repository full text, the DOI its only location); DSpace@MIT, searched for "hypercube Larson", which holds no copy of this paper or of its report version; the report version, New York City Rand Institute R-1238-HUD (March 1973), at https://www.rand.org/pubs/reports/R1238.html, which returned HTTP 403 with a CloudFront "Request blocked" page and was not retried; the NCJRS abstract page for it, which carries no abstract text, and https://www.ojp.gov/pdffiles1/Digitization/11696NCJRS.pdf, which returned 404; web searches for an author, course or institutional copy, which found none. Two neighbours stand in for it. Larson and Odoni's textbook, [LIT-2053](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2053.md), §§5.4–5.5 read in prose, restates the model (the busy/free state space on the vertices of an N-cube, geographical atoms, fixed-preference dispatch, the nine assumptions and the performance measures) and cites this paper for its generalizations and its computer-efficient solution. Hua, Luo, Swersey and Wen (2026), [LIT-2111](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2111.md), credit this paper specifically with the alternating hyperplane solution method and the TOUR algorithm. Neither stands in for the facility location and redistricting of its title, its numerical examples or its own statement of the method. |
| [LIT-2107](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2107.md) v2 | A Review of Incident Prediction, Resource Allocation, and Dispatch Models for Emergency Management | Mukhopadhyay et al. (2020). A review of approaches to emergency response management in four parts: incident prediction, incident detection, resource allocation and computer-aided dispatch. Only §6.1 was read. It says the seminal coverage models assume deterministic response, with "Resources at a facility are considered to be always available"; multiple coverage mitigates station unavailability, but modelling it needs probabilistic models, MEXCLP with one busy probability for every facility and MALP, whose second version computes busy fractions from local demand. | Active — read 2026-11-04 and 2026-11-06 (NOTE-1583, Read for §6.1) from arXiv v7: the opening of §6 and §6.1, "Coverage Models", with Table 1. Worth reading as a broad review of emergency response management (incident prediction, detection, resource allocation and dispatch), and in §6.1 for a short map of static coverage models, from the deterministic ones that treat a station's resources as always available, through multiple coverage, to the probabilistic ones that model station availability, MEXCLP, MALP and their extensions. Registered as a stand-in for Daskin (1983), [LIT-2098](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2098.md), and ReVelle and Hogan (1989), [LIT-2075](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2075.md), on those models' assumptions. Its main limits, as read: one-line summaries without formulas, which cannot confirm the papers' formulations; the rest of the review was not read. |
| [LIT-2111](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2111.md) v2 | A Geometrically Convergent Solution to Spatial Hypercube Queueing Models | Hua, Luo, Swersey & Wen (2026). The hypercube queueing model was built for homogeneous service rates; the authors extend it to server-specific rates with an exact solution through a birth–death process and an equivalent reformulation, show that their algorithm converges at a geometric rate, and parallelize it. On emergency medical service data they report the sequential algorithm over 1,000 times faster than a sparse solver and over 500 times faster than discrete-event simulation. They credit Larson (1974) with the model, the alternating hyperplane method and the TOUR algorithm. | Active — read 2026-11-06 (NOTE-1618, Read) from arXiv v2; worth reading as an exact solver for the spatial hypercube queueing model extended to server-specific service rates, by a birth–death decomposition and an equivalent reformulation with geometric convergence under a technical bound on how far the rates differ, parallelized, and as the clearest open statement of what Larson (1974) contributed: the alternating hyperplane solution method and the TOUR algorithm. Registered as a stand-in for Larson (1974), [LIT-2105](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2105.md), for the solution method only. Its main limits, as read: geometric convergence is proved for equal rates, and stated, with a gap in the proof, for unequal ones (THEORY-1426's note of 2026-11-06); the parallel algorithm and the speed-ups were skimmed, not checked; a preprint, with no journal version found. |
| [LIT-2114](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2114.md) v2 | The Connectivity of Boolean Satisfiability: Computational and Structural Dichotomies | Gopalan, Kolaitis, Maneva & Papadimitriou (2009). The solutions of a Boolean CNF(S)-formula, constants allowed, induce a subgraph of the hypercube, adjacent solutions differing in one variable. For a finite set S of relations: if S is tight (all componentwise bijunctive, all OR-free or all NAND-free), st-connectivity is in P, connectivity in coNP and component diameter linear; otherwise both are PSPACE-complete and diameter can be 2^Ω(√n). Tight sets properly contain Schaefer's tractable sets, so positive 1-in-3 SAT is NP-complete to satisfy but easy to navigate, while NAE-3SAT is hard for both. The hard side rests on faithful expressibility; the authors conjecture a trichotomy for connectivity. | Active — read in full 2026-11-06 ([NOTE-1584](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1584.md)) from arXiv v2, the proofs of the hard side (§§3.2–3.3) and of Lemmas 4.8–4.13 included; the SIAM version not compared, no discrepancy in a statement being named; worth reading as the first worst-case classification of how hard it is to navigate a solution space, across Boolean constraint languages: for a "tight" language st-connectivity under single-variable flips is in P and components have linear diameter, otherwise it is PSPACE-complete and diameter can be exponential. The boundary properly contains Schaefer's tractable classes and, by the authors' account, cuts across Boolean clones, so finding and navigating come apart in both directions. Its main limits: Boolean domain, constants allowed and single-flip moves only; and the easy side's boundary is slightly wrong, since repeated variables in constraints were not considered, as Schwerdtfeger (2014), [LIT-2027](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2027.md), shows and corrects to "safely tight"; the hard side as stated stands. |
| [LIT-2115](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2115.md) | A dichotomy theorem for nonuniform CSPs | Bulatov (2017). Proves the Feder–Vardi Dichotomy Conjecture: "For any finite constraint language Γ over a finite set the problem CSP(Γ) is either solvable in polynomial time or is NP-complete." Hardness was known; the contribution is a polynomial-time algorithm for every finite idempotent algebra with a weak near-unanimity term operation (equivalently, every algebra in HS(A) has a nontrivial term operation), and the algorithm is uniform in the algebra. It combines (2,3)-minimality with a new non-local condition, block-minimality, reached by decomposing instances along congruences, and with the few-subpowers algorithm, using separation of prime congruence intervals and a quasi-centralizer. | Active — read in part 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1572](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1572.md)) from arXiv v2, the 101-page full version; worth reading as one of the two independent proofs of the Feder–Vardi dichotomy: for a finite constraint language over a finite set, CSP(Γ) is in P or NP-complete, the tractable side being exactly the languages whose polymorphisms include a weak near-unanimity operation. Its clear §2 is the best short statement of how polymorphisms govern the complexity of a fixed-language CSP. Its main limits: finite domains only, decision only, nothing on moving between solutions, and a proof of some 80 pages (Part II, not checked here) whose v2 patches a gap in Lemma 46. |
